WASHINGTON (CNN) -- As he walks past the tiny, dingy waiting area into an equally cramped garage, Nui Srisook says business at his car repair shop is thriving. Drivers are choosing to keep their old cars longer, and they're turning to repair shops to make it so, observers say. Sales are up 20 percent this month and Srisook spends most nights working late, helping his customers to get extra mileage out of their old cars. "Most of the customers right now we see, they don't really have much extra money to ... buy a new car. So that's why they just do repair," Srisook said. "And now, people are willing to spend more money on maintaining the car, deciding what is broke, anything that needs to be maintained on the car." As more cash-strapped Americans turn to do-it-yourself projects and bargain shopping, car repair shops like Srisook's are feeling the boon. Drivers are choosing to keep their old cars longer, and often they're willing to put in the money to do so, observers say. The Automotive Service Association reports their members' sales were up 16 percent over last year.  Watch Kate Bolduan's report on the thriving auto repair industry » . "That indicated that people were coming in and putting the vehicle in the repair facilities' hands and saying, 'Look, I am going to be keeping this car. I want to be sure it runs well. I want to be sure that if there are any safety issues or any maintenance issues that I have overlooked, let's get those taken care of,' " said ASA President Ron Pyle. Pyle said that's a change from the past, when drivers would scrimp on the cost of maintenance and repair. "That was surprising news. We didn't expect that in the midst of the beginnings of the economic woes," Pyle said. "But they are looking at the cost of trying to purchase a new vehicle ... so I think that in relative terms that $1,000 repair to keep a $2,500 car running may be an attractive alternative." The economic slump has cut automakers deeply. Last month, sales of new cars were down more than 40 percent compared with the same time last year, according to sales tracker Autodata. The trend seems to have translated into increased traffic at auto parts stores. "We're doing way more business. The phones are ringing, you know, customers are walking in," said Darryl Wright, owner of D.C. Brake & Bearings Co. "Basically, if it's broke, they fix it." In the past, only savvy auto mechanics knew to shop at Wright's nondescript discount store. Now, he sees more car owners who are looking for a cheaper deal on parts. "[Customers will] find a guy on the street, you know -- Joe Shady Mechanics is what we call them -- to fix it at a deeper discount rate, labor-wise, and they'll send the customer in here to buy the parts on their own," Wright said. "So people are saving money that way too." Srisook said he keeps service prices low to appeal to those bargain shoppers, such as Esther White, a loyal customer. She brought in her daughter's 1996 Oldsmobile for new rotors and brakes, and said her daughter would be driving the car "until it drops dead." "Believe it or not, we were raised to fix things, and to hold on to things as long as we could," White said. "But it goes back to today's economy, and making the right financial decisions."

# The Repair Shop Boom: How Economic Pressures Are Changing American Car Ownership

As the economy continues to weigh heavily on household budgets, an unexpected beneficiary has emerged: the auto repair industry. Nui Srisook, owner of a local car repair shop, reports that business has never been better, with sales climbing an impressive 20 percent this month alone. Her experience reflects a broader trend sweeping across the automotive service sector nationwide.

The reasoning behind this surge is straightforward but significant. Cash-strapped drivers, facing tighter budgets and economic uncertainty, are making a deliberate choice to extend the life of their current vehicles rather than take on the financial burden of purchasing new ones. Instead of trading in older cars, these consumers are opting to invest in repairs and maintenance, viewing this as a more financially sound decision during uncertain economic times.

This shift isn't isolated to individual shops like Srisook's—it represents an industry-wide pattern. The Automotive Service Association (ASA), a leading trade organization, reports that its members have seen sales increase by 16 percent compared to the previous year, further confirming that Srisook's experience is part of a larger, measurable trend affecting repair businesses across the country.

Perhaps more telling than the sales figures themselves is the change in customer behavior and priorities. ASA President Ron Pyle has observed a notable shift in how consumers approach vehicle maintenance. Where drivers once might have cut corners or delayed necessary repairs to save money, they are now prioritizing thorough, comprehensive service and safety-related maintenance. This represents a departure from previous economic downturns, when scrimping on car upkeep was often the default response to financial pressure.

Pyle offers a compelling explanation for this behavioral shift, framing it in terms of straightforward economic logic: spending approximately $1,000 to repair a car valued at $2,500 has become an increasingly attractive option compared to purchasing a new vehicle. In the current economic climate, this math makes sense to many consumers who are looking for ways to stretch their dollars further while still maintaining reliable transportation.

Together, these observations paint a picture of an automotive repair industry that is thriving precisely because of broader economic challenges. As drivers recalculate the cost-benefit analysis of repair versus replacement, repair shops like Srisook's are experiencing a welcome boost in business—demonstrating how economic downturns can create unexpected opportunities even as they present challenges elsewhere in the economy.

# The Great American Car Repair Boom: How Economic Hardship is Reviving an Old Industry

As the economic downturn tightens its grip on household finances across the nation, millions of Americans are making a pragmatic choice that's reshaping the automotive landscape: rather than trading in their aging vehicles for shiny new models, they're choosing to repair, maintain, and extend the life of the cars they already own. This shift in consumer behavior, driven largely by necessity rather than preference, has become a lifeline for auto repair shops nationwide, many of which had struggled during previous economic cycles when car sales boomed and repair work seemed less essential.

The numbers tell a compelling story. Auto repair businesses across the country are reporting sales increases ranging from 16 to 20 percent, a remarkable surge that stands in stark contrast to the struggles facing new car dealerships during this same period. While showrooms sit relatively quiet and car manufacturers grapple with declining sales figures, the service bays and repair garages are humming with activity, filled with customers seeking oil changes, brake repairs, transmission work, and other maintenance services that keep their existing vehicles roadworthy.

This trend reflects a broader psychological and financial shift among American consumers. When faced with the choice between spending several hundred dollars on repairs versus tens of thousands of dollars on a new vehicle purchase—complete with monthly loan payments, higher insurance premiums, and depreciation costs—cash-strapped families are increasingly recognizing that keeping their current car running represents the more fiscally responsible choice. A vehicle that might have been traded in during more prosperous times is now being kept for an additional two, three, or even five years, with owners investing in the necessary repairs to keep it functional and safe.

For auto repair shop owners, this represents an unexpected silver lining amid otherwise challenging economic conditions. Many have seen their customer base expand as word spreads about their ability to breathe new life into older vehicles at a fraction of the cost of replacement. Mechanics who specialize in diagnosing and fixing problems in higher-mileage vehicles are finding themselves particularly busy, as customers who once might have simply traded in a car with a check engine light now seek expert diagnosis and repair.

This behavioral shift also speaks to a broader recalibration of American consumer priorities during economic uncertainty. Rather than viewing car ownership through the lens of status or the desire for the latest features and technology, budget-conscious consumers are adopting a more utilitarian perspective: a car's primary function is transportation, and if that function can be preserved through strategic maintenance and repair, the additional expense of a new vehicle becomes difficult to justify. This mindset extends beyond just the immediate financial savings—it also reflects a growing awareness of the total cost of ownership, including how quickly new vehicles depreciate in their first few years and the long-term financial commitment that comes with auto loans.

The ripple effects of this trend extend throughout the automotive service industry ecosystem. Parts suppliers are seeing increased demand for components needed in older vehicles, from specialty parts for discontinued models to more common items like batteries, belts, and hoses. Independent repair shops, in particular, appear to be benefiting from this trend, as consumers seek out potentially lower-cost alternatives to dealership service departments while still expecting quality workmanship.

As this pattern continues, it raises interesting questions about long-term shifts in American car ownership culture. While economic downturns have historically been temporary, the habits and financial lessons learned during these periods—including a renewed appreciation for vehicle maintenance and the value of extending a car's lifespan—may well outlast the current economic challenges, potentially reshaping consumer relationships with car ownership for years to come.

counterfactuals.output:
# As New Car Sales Stall, Repair Shops Rev Up Business

**By CNN Business Staff**

Across the country, auto repair shops are experiencing an unexpected side effect of economic uncertainty: business is booming, even as new car dealerships struggle to move inventory off their lots.

With household budgets tightening and consumer confidence wavering, Americans are increasingly choosing to repair aging vehicles rather than take on new auto loans. The shift is providing a lifeline to independent mechanics and repair chains nationwide, even as broader economic indicators flash warning signs.

"We've seen a noticeable uptick over the past several months," said Marcus Chen, who owns a repair shop in suburban Columbus, Ohio. "People who might have traded in their car for something newer are now asking us to keep their current vehicle running for another two or three years."

## Aging Fleet, Growing Demand

Industry data shows the average age of vehicles on American roads has been climbing steadily, a trend that appears to be accelerating amid economic pressures. Higher interest rates on auto loans, combined with concerns about job security, are pushing consumers to extend the life of their current cars rather than finance new purchases.

"When people are worried about their financial future, deferring a major purchase like a new car is one of the first adjustments they make," said Sarah Whitfield, an economist who tracks consumer spending patterns. "But that car still needs to run, so repair and maintenance spending often holds steady or even increases during downturns."

Major repair chains are reporting the trend in their earnings calls, with several citing increased same-store sales even as new vehicle sales figures decline nationally. Auto parts retailers have echoed the sentiment, noting stronger demand for both DIY repair components and professional service parts.

## A Familiar Pattern

Economists note this isn't the first time repair shops have benefited from economic downturns. Similar patterns emerged during the 2008 financial crisis, when new car sales plummeted while service bays stayed busy.

"There's a countercyclical element to auto repair," Whitfield explained. "It's one of those industries that can actually see tailwinds when the broader economy is struggling, because people are making do with what they have rather than buying new."

For shop owners like Chen, the increased business comes with mixed feelings.

"I'm glad to have the work, don't get me wrong," he said. "But I know a lot of these customers are stretching their budgets thin just to keep their car on the road. It's not exactly a sign that things are going great."

## Looking Ahead

Industry analysts caution that the boost may have limits. If economic conditions worsen significantly, even routine maintenance and repairs could become discretionary expenses that cash-strapped consumers delay or skip altogether.

For now, though, many repair shops are capitalizing on the moment, some even expanding staff to meet demand—a rare bright spot of hiring in an otherwise cautious economic landscape.

*This story reflects general economic trends and is not tied to a specific reporting period.*

# When the Going Gets Tough, Americans Get Under the Hood

**Local Repair Shops See Business Boom as Drivers Choose Fixes Over New Car Payments**

MAPLEWOOD — On a Tuesday morning that smells like motor oil and coffee, Frank Delgado slides out from under a 2011 Honda Accord with 187,000 miles on it and delivers news that would have sent most customers running to a dealership a decade ago.

"Timing belt, water pump, and your rear brakes are getting thin," he tells Maria Sanchez, who's been waiting in the cramped lobby of Delgado's Auto Repair for two hours. "We're looking at about $1,100."

Sanchez doesn't flinch. "Do it," she says. "This car and I are in a long-term relationship."

Across the country, that sentiment is becoming the new normal. As economic uncertainty tightens household budgets, more Americans are choosing to repair aging vehicles rather than take on new car payments—a shift that's reshaping the auto industry and keeping mechanics like Delgado busier than ever.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

The average age of vehicles on American roads has climbed to a record high, according to automotive research firm S&P Global Mobility, with cars and light trucks averaging over 12 years old. New car prices, meanwhile, have surged well past pre-pandemic levels, with the average transaction price hovering around $48,000—a number that feels increasingly out of reach for many families.

"I used to see maybe two customers a week asking if their car was 'worth fixing,'" says Delgado, who's run his shop for 23 years. "Now it's every single day. People aren't asking if they *should* fix it anymore. They're asking how much it costs, period."

## A Different Kind of Customer

Sanchez, a 34-year-old elementary school teacher, says the math simply doesn't work in favor of buying new.

"A car payment would be $400, $500 a month easy, plus higher insurance," she says. "I can put a lot of money into keeping this Honda running before I hit that number. My dad always said Hondas run forever if you take care of them. I'm testing that theory."

She's not alone. In Ohio, retired postal worker Gene Whitfield just paid $2,300 to rebuild the transmission in his 2009 Ford F-150.

"My neighbor said I was crazy, said I should've just bought a used truck," Whitfield says, laughing. "But a decent used truck runs $20,000 now for something with 80,000 miles already on it. I know every inch of this truck. I know what's been replaced. That's worth something."

## Mechanics See a Shift in Mindset

For shop owners, the change isn't just about volume—it's about the kinds of conversations they're having with customers.

"Five years ago, if I told someone their repair would cost more than 50% of the car's value, they'd usually just trade it in," says Denise Okafor, who owns a repair shop in suburban Atlanta. "Now people do the math differently. They're asking, 'What will a replacement cost me, really—not just the sticker price, but insurance, registration, the loan interest?' When you add it all up, keeping the old car often wins."

Okafor has noticed something else too: customers are becoming more invested in preventive maintenance.

"People who used to skip oil changes are now religious about them," she says. "They finally understand that a $60 oil change is a lot cheaper than a $4,000 engine job. This economy is teaching people to actually take care of their stuff."

## The Emotional Math

For many customers, the decision isn't purely financial—it's also about avoiding the stress of another monthly bill in uncertain times.

"I don't want to be locked into a five- or six-year loan when I don't know what next year looks like," says Sanchez. "If something happens with my job, I can always park this car for a month if I need to. Try doing that with a car payment."

That sentiment resonates with Delgado, who says he's started having more honest conversations with customers about their options.

"I could always push people toward a new car—tell them the repair isn't worth it, send them to a dealership," he says. "But that's not the business I want to run. If I can get someone another two years out of a car that's paid off, I've saved them real money. Word gets around when you're straight with people."

## Built to Last, One Repair at a Time

Back in the shop, as Sanchez heads out to arrange a ride home while her Accord goes up on the lift, she reflects on what her aging car has come to represent.

"It's not glamorous," she says. "It's got a dent in the bumper and the AC makes a weird noise sometimes. But it's mine, it's paid for, and every time I fix something, I'm investing in something I already own instead of starting over."

For Delgado, watching customers make that calculation has become the new rhythm of his workday.

"People aren't just fixing cars," he says, wiping his hands on a rag as he heads back to the Accord. "They're making a statement about what matters to them right now. And what matters is stability—not shiny."

---

*This is a fictional composite story created for illustrative purposes. Names, shops, and specific details are not drawn from real individuals or events, though they reflect broader economic trends reported by outlets like S&P Global Mobility and industry analysts.*

# As New Car Sales Stall, Americans Turn to Repair Shops to Keep Old Vehicles Running

**Auto service industry sees revenue surge as consumers delay big-ticket purchases**

---Detroit, MI---

At a time when new car dealerships across the country report significant sales declines, an unlikely beneficiary has emerged from the economic downturn: the local auto repair shop.

Independent mechanics, franchise repair chains, and dealership service departments are reporting notable upticks in business as consumers who might otherwise be shopping for new vehicles instead choose to repair and maintain their current cars.

"Business has never been better," said one shop owner in the Midwest, describing waiting lists that stretch out for days. "People who used to trade in their cars every three or four years are now asking us to help them get another 50,000 miles out of what they've got."

## A Shift in Consumer Behavior

Industry analysts point to a straightforward explanation: with credit tighter, job security uncertain, and household budgets strained, big-ticket purchases like new vehicles have become harder to justify. The average age of vehicles on American roads has been climbing, and that aging fleet requires more frequent maintenance and repair.

Trade groups representing the auto parts and repair sector have noted increased demand for a range of services — from routine maintenance like brake jobs and tire replacements to more significant repairs involving transmissions and engines that owners might have previously avoided by simply purchasing a new car.

Retailers specializing in auto parts have also reported stronger sales, as more consumers opt to tackle repairs themselves or supply their trusted mechanics directly.

## Dealerships Adapt

Some new car dealerships, facing steep declines in showroom traffic, have shifted focus toward their service departments to shore up revenue. Several have expanded service hours and marketing efforts aimed at existing customers, hoping to offset losses from the sales floor.

"We're seeing customers who bought cars from us five or six years ago come back — not to buy, but to fix what they have," said a dealership service manager. "It's not the business model we built around, but it's keeping the lights on."

## A Familiar Pattern

Economists note that this dynamic — consumers repairing rather than replacing during downturns — is a familiar pattern in recessionary periods, though the scale of the current shift reflects the severity of the broader economic crisis. Tight lending conditions have made auto loans harder to secure for many buyers, while economic uncertainty has made even qualified buyers hesitant to take on new debt.

For now, the trend offers a rare bright spot in an otherwise difficult economic landscape for the broader auto industry — even as manufacturers and dealerships continue to grapple with the steep decline in new vehicle sales nationwide.

---
*This report reflects industry trends observed during a period of broader economic difficulty affecting the automotive sector.*

"When people hold onto their cars longer, that directly translates into more service and repair work," said the association's chief economist in a recent statement. "We're seeing steady growth across nearly every repair category—from routine maintenance to major component replacement."

The association's data shows that shops specializing in older-vehicle repairs—transmission work, suspension systems, and electrical diagnostics—have seen some of the strongest demand increases, with some categories reporting double-digit growth in service volume.

## A View from the Shop Floor

For independent shop owners, the numbers translate into real changes on the ground. Maria Delgado, who has run Delgado's Auto Repair in a mid-sized Midwestern city for the past 15 years, says she's booking appointments two to three weeks out—a first for her business.

"Five years ago, I might have a slow Tuesday where I'm just doing oil changes and hoping the phone rings," Delgado said. "Now I've had to hire two more technicians just to keep up. People are calling me instead of calling their dealership's finance department."

Delgado said many of her customers are explicit about their reasoning. "They tell me straight up: 'I looked at buying new, saw the payment, and decided to fix what I've got instead.' I'm hearing that constantly."

She's also noticed a shift in the type of work coming through her bay doors. "We're doing more transmission rebuilds, more major engine work—stuff people used to just trade in the car for. Now they want it to last another five years."

## Looking Ahead

Industry analysts caution that the repair sector's growth, while robust, faces its own pressures—including rising costs for parts and a persistent shortage of qualified technicians. Still, for shop owners like Delgado, the immediate outlook remains positive.

"I'm not complaining," she said with a laugh. "But I could use a few more good mechanics if anyone's looking."

# Americans Keep Cars Longer as Costs Push Buyers Away From Showrooms

**WASHINGTON** — On a side street a few blocks from the Capitol, mechanic Ray Delgado has noticed a shift in the vehicles rolling into his three-bay garage. The cars are older. The customers are more insistent about getting one more year out of them. And they're asking more questions about used parts before agreeing to any repair.

"Five years ago, somebody would come in with a check engine light and a 2015 with 140,000 miles, and half the time they'd say, 'Just tell me if it's worth fixing,'" said Delgado, who has run his shop for 22 years. "Now everybody wants it fixed. Nobody's trading it in. They can't afford what's on the lot."

Across the country, a similar calculation is playing out in driveways and garages as the average price of a new vehicle hovers near $48,000 and auto loan rates remain elevated, pricing many buyers out of the new-car market entirely. The result is a growing population of consumers choosing repair over replacement — and increasingly turning to independent parts stores and aftermarket components to keep aging vehicles running.

Industry data reflects the trend. The average age of vehicles on American roads climbed past 12.5 years in recent tracking by S&P Global Mobility, a record and a marked increase from just over a decade ago. Auto parts retailers, meanwhile, have reported steady growth even as new-vehicle sales have cooled, a divergence analysts say reflects a durable shift in consumer behavior rather than a temporary blip.

"When new vehicle prices go up and interest rates stay elevated, the math changes for a huge share of households," said Melinda Cho, an economist who studies consumer durables at a Washington-based research firm. "People aren't just delaying a purchase for a few months. They're re-engineering their whole relationship with their car. They're asking, 'How do I make this last another three years,' instead of 'When do I trade it in.'"

That re-engineering is visible at auto parts counters nationwide, where store employees say they've seen more first-time do-it-yourselfers alongside longtime hobbyists. Chains have leaned into the trend, expanding online diagnostic tools, offering free battery testing and code-reading services, and stocking more remanufactured components — alternators, starters, brake calipers — at lower price points than new original-equipment parts.

"We get people who've genuinely never changed their own oil before standing in the aisle looking up YouTube videos," said a manager at a parts store in suburban Maryland, who asked not to be named because he wasn't authorized to speak to the press. "The instinct used to be: something's wrong, go look at new cars. Now it's: something's wrong, go look at what it costs to fix it, and can I do it myself or find a cheaper independent shop."

Independent repair shops, once squeezed by dealership service departments and extended factory warranties, say they are benefiting from the shift as well. Trade groups representing independent mechanics report that referral traffic and average repair-order volumes are up, even as some customers stretch out payment plans or ask shops to prioritize the most urgent fix and defer the rest.

The trend carries costs of its own. Older vehicles require more frequent maintenance, and repair bills — driven up by the same supply-chain and labor pressures affecting the broader economy — are not cheap either. Consumers who once might have absorbed a $2,000 repair by simply buying a new car are instead financing that repair, sometimes through the same buy-now-pay-later services reshaping other corners of retail.

Automakers are watching the trend closely. Slower turnover in the used and new vehicle pipeline can tighten inventory further down the road and complicate demand forecasts for manufacturers already navigating higher production costs. Some industry analysts argue the pattern could prove self-reinforcing: as more Americans keep vehicles longer, used-car values could firm up, making it costlier still for budget-conscious buyers to trade into anything newer, further entrenching the repair-first mindset.

For now, in shops like Delgado's, the calculus remains straightforward for the people writing the checks.

"Nobody wants a car payment on top of everything else going up," said Teresa Nunley, who brought her 2011 sedan in for a transmission repair rather than consider a replacement. "This car is paid off. I'd rather put $1,800 into it than take on a $600-a-month loan. That's just real math."

Delgado nodded along as she spoke, then turned back to the car up on his lift — another one, he said, that would probably outlive its warranty by a decade.
